title: Wang Yangming: On Fixing One's Resolve
excerpt: Excerpt from The Sage of the Mind: Wang Yangming by Xu Baoyun

inline.s: Excerpt from The Sage of the Mind: Wang Yangming by Xu Baoyun.
The one unrivalled gateway to the accomplishment of any undertaking.

One day Wang Shouren was sitting at ease with his disciples in a grove before Mount Langya, teacher and students discoursing together on learning in an atmosphere of perfect leisure. Among them Xu Ai asked a question: "May I ask, sir, what is the single most important matter in a person's life?"

Xu Ai, whose courtesy name was Yueren, was Wang Shouren's brother-in-law. Because of this family connection Xu Ai enjoyed the vantage of the waterfront tower that first catches the moonlight — he became Wang Shouren's earliest disciple and his first student. Xu Ai loved to mull over questions, and the one he asked today

sounded to most people quite vague and therefore hard to answer. Yet Wang Shouren happened to have turned this very matter over carefully in his mind long ago and had already thought it through. Now that Xu Ai asked him, Wang Shouren answered without a moment's thought: "The most important thing in life is to fix one's resolve. If the resolve is not fixed, nothing in the world can be accomplished."
Wang Shouren stated this so plainly and decisively that the students at once perked up
Xu Ai hastened to ask: "And what, sir, is this 'resolve' you speak of?"

Wang Shouren thought briefly: "What we call resolve is the ideal and goal a person sets for himself; it is also the point where one's learning gains traction. All of us who study through cold windows, thinking with all our might and earnestly practicing this work of self-restraint — what is the final purpose of it all? This must be made clear in the mind from the very start. Once it is clear, once you know what you are about, and then act upon it, you will have spirit, and only then can you succeed. It is like planting a tree: first the roots must be set firmly in the soil, made steady and secure, and only then can the tree grow. Many people are no longer young and have read a great deal, yet if you suddenly ask them, 'What is your life's ideal? What resolve have you set?' they are struck speechless and cannot answer; or they prattle some tedious nonsense and try to laugh the question off; or they speak of renouncing the world, of cultivation, of emptiness, stillness, and nothingness — dispirited, useless talk. Such people are without ideals and have fixed no resolve."
At Master Yangming's explanation the students all nodded one after another. Xu Ai asked again: "That one should fix a resolve in life is indeed essential, but what
kind of
resolve ought one to set?"

Xu Ai's question was an interesting one, and Wang Shouren answered with a smile: "In the matter of resolve, the greater the better, the higher the better. The ancients said: 'Model yourself on the highest and you will attain only the middle; model yourself on the middle and you will attain only the lowest.' This saying is not entirely true, yet it can serve as a point of reference. Therefore one must set a great resolve. I hold that he who resolves to be a sage can become a sage, and he who resolves to be a worthy can become a worthy!"
These words of Wang Shouren's
rang out with resounding force,
and at once someone nearby asked: "Sir, could you tell us something of the benefits of fixing one's resolve?"
Confucius once said: "Lift up one corner, and you should come back with the other three." What he meant was
that
if students truly concentrate while listening to a lecture, then the master makes one point and the students raise three questions, and it is between question and answer that learning arises.

Now that Wang Shouren was discoursing here on learning and his disciples were interjecting, and since they had at once touched the vital point, it was plain they were listening in earnest. Greatly pleased, Wang Shouren said immediately: "What we Confucian scholars study is none other than the 'learning of the noble person,' and this learning regards the fixing of resolve as its foremost concern at all times and in all places. Have you ever watched a cat pounce upon a mouse? At that moment
the cat is wholly absorbed — its eyes
watching,
its ears
listening,
its mind
thinking —

all on that one thing alone, seeing nothing else, hearing nothing else, thinking of nothing else. Only thus can our spirit become concentrated, our understanding of principle become profound, and our experience of innate knowing become clear. If we keep this up until it becomes habit, then whenever a selfish desire or stray thought arises in the mind, we will at once ask ourselves: 'How can such a thought arise? Do I still want my resolve to become a sage or a worthy, or not?' And the moment we press the question, the selfish, deviant thought recedes. When we feel like slacking off in our studies, we likewise ask ourselves at once: 'Do I still want this resolve, or not?' One such question, and the lazy impulse subsides. In this way our learning grows ever more diligent while selfish and deviant thoughts grow ever fewer, and after several years of persistence our learning will have advanced."
Wang Shouren had spoken to this point, and the disciple who had asked now understood: "What
the master

describes sounds like the meaning of that saying, 'In the pursuit of learning one increases day by day; in the pursuit of the Dao one decreases day by day, decreasing and decreasing again until one reaches non-action.'"
Wang Shouren nodded: "Precisely that meaning. In study one must not be
lazy

but must progress day by day. In clearing away the selfish desires within the mind one must also not be lazy, but must diminish them day by day, less and less, until one reaches 'non-action' — that is, until such deviant thoughts no longer arise. To truly accomplish this is indeed admirable."
Having said this, he returned once more to the earlier topic

"So the two words 'fix the resolve' are of vital importance, and above all one must fix the great resolve to 'become a sage.' In this way, whenever any deviant thought arises — laziness, negligence, envy, resentment, irascibility, greed, stinginess, arrogance, and all manner of unwholesome notions — the moment it arises, innate knowing detects it at once. At such a time do not hesitate in the least, do not be indulgent in the slightest, but confront yourself head-on and ask: 'Do I still want my great resolve to become a sage or not?' And in an instant these thoughts are struck down. It is just like the principle that once the sun comes out
the haze
is swept clean in a moment — what is there to doubt about this?"

Hearing Wang Shouren's words, none of the disciples could refrain from nodding. Xiao Hui, who sat beside Xu Ai, was the first to applaud and exclaim: "Well said, Master! From the very day I came to your side I resolved that I must fix a great resolve, so as not to fail this life!"

Xiao Hui's words were most forceful, but Wang Shouren knew that Xiao Hui was rather flighty in conduct and not solid enough. Now that his mouth moved faster than anyone's and his voice rang louder than anyone's, Wang Shouren could not help saying to him with a smile: "I believe it when you say you have fixed a resolve, but I fear what you have resolved upon is not the great resolve to become a sage."

With this one remark Master Yangming set all the disciples laughing. Xiao Hui, at a loss and somewhat embarrassed, hastened to bow with folded hands and ask: "This student does truly aspire to learning and is willing to fix a resolve; I simply do not know how to begin. May I ask you, sir, for a word of guidance?"

Wang Shouren knew that Xiao Hui was in fact very intelligent, only that his mind was full of sundry and confused thoughts, so he said gravely: "Let me tell you a story. There was a student who traveled a thousand miles to seek me out, for the sole purpose of asking about 'the way to become a sage'

I told him the single word 'resolve,' and beyond that there was nothing more to say. The student was not satisfied and pressed further. So I asked him: 'Your journey here could not have been easy. Did you meet with any hardship?' At these words the student launched into an endless account of his travels — the toil of boat and carriage, the scorching heat and poisonous sun, and his extraordinary suffering. Halfway along, his traveling money ran short, so he gave his last few coins to his servant and went to borrow grain from an acquaintance himself. As he spoke on, even I felt sorry for him

Yet the student said: 'To be able to see your face, Master, and to consult you about learning — I feel only joy, and not the least hardship.' So I said to him: 'You aspire to learning, and I have further given you the great guiding idea of fixing the resolve to become a sage — that is already enough.' The student then asked about the concrete method of 'becoming a sage,' and I told him: 'Why must you insist on asking about the process of realizing an ideal? So long as you fix the great resolve to become a sage and push on with undivided effort, that is enough. For example, when you set out from home to come here and consult me about learning, the road was so difficult and no one forced you to come, yet you still pressed on, step by step, on your own two feet
Crossing mountains and fording rivers

enduring the toil of boat and cart — had it not been for the pursuit of learning, I doubt you would have come out to suffer such hardship. But now you have resolved upon learning, and so you traveled a thousand miles to see me, asking your way whenever you did not know the road, finding a means to overcome every difficulty, persevering step by step until at last you reached me. And now, far from feeling the journey arduous, you feel only delight. This is because you fixed a resolve and found a point of leverage; you naturally applied yourself, and where effort is applied, there is bound to be a harvest. The road to sagehood is the same. I often tell my students: 'The way of the sage is wholly sufficient in our own nature.' You yourself possess this kind of perseverance; take this perseverance and make it your learning. So long as you hold fast to your resolve and never let go, and walk on step by step, what undertaking will not succeed? This — this is the way!'"

Of Wang Shouren's words, some of the listening disciples understood, and some understood half, and all could not help nodding in agreement. Yet it was the cleverest of them, Xiao Hui, who was dullest on this point, unable to grasp it at all, and he asked again: "Could the master explain it a little more plainly?"

Such is the way of the world: those who appear the cleverest are often the most confused on great matters of right and wrong. Faced with Xiao Hui, Master Yangming was for a moment at a loss for words, and could only say: "I have already said all there is to say. How is it that you still do not understand?"

What Master Yangming imparted was the one unrivalled gateway to the accomplishment of any undertaking. He truly carried the method by which people of the world realize their ideals to its deepest point and put it into the most practical terms. Whoever one may be, so long as one acts upon this method in earnest, realizing one's life's ideal will not prove too difficult.
If, having come this far, one still does not understand, then the matter is truly hard to set right.
